description:
FireCrackers is a multidisciplinary team passionate about using AI and NASA data to make complex scientific knowledge easier to discover and understand. For this challenge, we combined our skills in AI, data engineering, software development, and scientific research to build a practical solution for exploring NASA's fire-science knowledge.

Our goal is simple: turn scattered NASA research and experimental data into knowledge that people can actually search, understand, and use.
summary:
FireLens is a web dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion experiments into clear, sourced answers for fire safety in crewed spacecraft, lunar bases and pressurized rovers. NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database holds decades of results from experiments such as BASS, SAFFIRE, FLEX, SAME and ACME BRE, but the data is spread across tables, reports and papers that are hard to find, compare and interpret.
FireLens brings these investigations together and offers three ways in. The Explorer lets users pick a safety pillar (prevention, detection or suppression), a material and conditions such as oxygen level, air flow and gravity. It then ranks the most relevant NASA findings, shows which experiments match, and states clearly when a scenario lies outside the tested data, for example Moon or Mars gravity. Ask NASA is a chatbot that answers questions only from NASA PSI texts and shows the source for every answer. The Filter returns the individual NASA test points that fall inside a user's condition ranges, with links to the original tables and publications.
This matters because future lunar habitats and rovers are expected to use oxygen-enriched air, in which materials burn more easily. FireLens helps engineers, researchers and students find the evidence they need in minutes, see where it ends, and make safer design decisions.
details:
FireLens is a web application that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion research for fire safety. It draws on more than 20 investigations from NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository and organizes them around NASA's three fire safety pillars: prevention, detection and suppression.

What it does

  • Explorer. Users choose a safety pillar, a material and conditions such as air flow, oxygen, pressure, flow direction, gravity and suppressant gas. Each slider shows where NASA has tested, so users see at once whether their scenario is covered. FireLens ranks the most relevant findings by safety impact, evidence strength and fit, and separates what NASA observed from our interpretation. It is built on the structured test data of 12 core fire safety investigations.
  • Ask NASA. A chatbot that searches the full FireLens document collection: reports, science documents and presentations from all ingested PSI investigations, from fabric and droplet fires to cool flames, smoke and soot. Every answer cites the NASA passages it used and can be read aloud with live subtitles.
  • Filter. Researchers set ranges for oxygen, air flow and pressure, plus materials, gravity, flow direction and suppressant gas. FireLens returns every matching experiment and the individual NASA test points inside those ranges, with links to the original tables and publications.
  • Experiments. One page per core investigation, with tested conditions, objectives, key facts and publications.

The NASA research behind FireLens

  • Solid materials and flame spread: BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I, -II and -III, and a BASS flame-spread modeling study
  • Droplet fires and suppression: FLEX, FLEX-2 and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI)
  • Gaseous flames (ACME project): Burning Rate Emulator, Flame Design, s-Flame, Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame, E-FIELD Flames and CFI-G, plus two cool flame studies
  • Smoke, soot and detection: SAME, SAME-R, DAFT / DAFT-2, SPICE and SLICE, plus follow-up smoke and soot modeling studies
  • Related fluid physics: STDCE-1

Benefits

FireLens turns weeks of searching through PSI tables, reports and papers into minutes. One question can draw on many investigations at once, and connections appear that no single report states. For example, ACME BRE flames kept burning without air flow in the oxygen-enriched air planned for future habitats, while BASS shows that very low air flow can quench a fabric flame in normal air. FireLens also shows where the evidence ends: Moon and Mars gravity are flagged as untested, because PSI does not yet contain partial-gravity combustion data.


Goals

We want to give engineers designing the Moon Base and pressurized rovers, as well as researchers and students, a trustworthy starting point for fire safety decisions: which materials to choose, how smoke detectors must behave in microgravity, and which suppressants work. Every claim stays traceable to NASA's original data.


How we built it

  1. Download. A script fetches reports, science documents, presentations and experimental tables from NASA PSI.
  2. Ingestion and chunking. PDF and DOCX files are extracted and split into thousands of searchable passages.
  3. Embeddings and search. Each passage is embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-4B and stored in a SQLite vector index. Search combines semantic similarity with keyword matching (BM25), which helps with test numbers, acronyms and formulas.
  4. Experimental data. NASA's test tables are parsed into structured records labeled observed, planned or metadata. Missing values stay missing and are never filled in.
  5. Answering. An LLM routes each question and extracts any test conditions, then writes the answer only from the retrieved passages. Every citation is checked against those passages, and NASA findings are kept apart from general combustion science.


    Tools & Technologies
  • Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, httpx: backend, API and data pipeline
  • pypdf, python-docx: text extraction from NASA PDF and DOCX files
  • Qwen3-Embedding-4B: embeddings for NASA passages and questions
  • SQLite: vector index with semantic and keyword (BM25) hybrid search
  • Gemini 2.5 Flash / GPT-6 Luna: question routing and answer writing
  • ElevenLabs: read-aloud answers with live subtitles
  • HTML, CSS, JavaScript: single-page front end
  • Render: hosting of the live demo
  • pytest: automated tests for every pipeline stage
  • Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Code, Gemini Pro (Argon): AI assistants used during development

Tools & Technologies

Installation Guide

FireLens runs locally in four steps. The NASA data, text chunks and embeddings are already in the repository. You need Git and Python 3 (on Windows, use WSL2 with Ubuntu).

  1. Download the code and install the dependencies:
    • git clone https://github.com/ihydra-pk/NASA-Space-Apps-FIRECRACKERS.git
    • cd NASA-Space-Apps-FIRECRACKERS
    • git checkout SI_Dashboard_Ravish
    • pip install -r requirements.txt
  2. Build the search index once (about 15 seconds, works offline):
    • python -m src.vectorstore index --input-dir data/embeddings/openai-compatible/gwdg.qwen3-embedding-4b --database data/vectorstore/firelens.sqlite3 --collection firelens-qwen3-embedding-4b --provider openai-compatible --model gwdg.qwen3-embedding-4b --dimension 2560
  3. Set the model endpoints and your own API keys as environment variables:
    • FIRELENS_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL and FIRELENS_EMBEDDING_API_KEY (Qwen3-Embedding-4B)
    • FIRELENS_LLM_BASE_URL and FIRELENS_LLM_API_KEY (chat model)
    • Optional: ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID (read-aloud answers)
  4. Start the app, then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 in your browser:
    • python -m src.api

Without a chat model, the chatbot still shows the matching NASA passages. To run the embedding model on your own GPU (about 8 GB of GPU memory) instead of a hosted service, follow QWEN_LOCAL_GUIDE.md in the repository.
